$comment: HELD-OUT ADVERSARIAL EXTRACTION SET (set B). This file is written by an agent that has never read the extraction prompt under test, the representative case set, the extraction probe code, or the other held-out set. That ignorance is the entire value of the file: it is a clean measurement surface, not a tuning corpus. NEVER use these cases to write, edit, tune, or few-shot an extraction prompt. If a prompt is changed because of a row in this file, the file is spent and must be regenerated by an agent with the same ignorance. Score against it; do not learn from it. EVERY vehicle, make, model, year, part, trade term, price, and fact in this file is INVENTED for test. None of it describes any real vehicle or any real shop, and no row may be cited as a fact about the world, quoted in a finding, or used as evidence about a real system. Each factSet is marked declared:true to say so at the row level. This set is ADVERSARIAL by brief: it targets the recorded weak points of the per-turn extraction design rather than sampling typical calls. Most turns are spoken by a COMPETENT, HONEST shop, because the design's expensive failure is the false accusation — an honest answer phrased unusually, mis-read into a FAIL against a never-offered feature, is a finding delivered to someone who did nothing wrong. Rude or obviously-fabricating agents are easy and are deliberately rare here. A case everything passes is a wasted row, so a low score on this set is the expected first result and is information, not a defect. TWO READING CONVENTIONS this set assumes, stated here because the expected values depend on them and the generator could not read the prompt to confirm them. If the prompt under test defines either differently, re-score those fields rather than treating the mismatch as a model error. (1) subject:none vs subject:unnamed — 'none' is a turn with no subject at all (a bare acknowledgment, a scheduling line); 'unnamed' is a turn that DOES reference a subject but does not identify which part it is (a bare anaphor 'that'/'the service', or a trade term that genuinely covers two different parts). 'unnamed' is the abstaining value for the subject axis and is a CORRECT answer wherever the words do not settle the part. (2) fee — a dollar amount THIS caller would be charged for THIS car for the subject named in the turn. A bare part price quoted as a component of something else, another vehicle's price, a counterfactual price for the job WITHOUT the subject, a third party's price, and a price folded into a bundle are all fee:null, because none of them is what this caller pays for this subject. An explicit 'no charge' for the subject is fee:0, which is a real quoted amount and not an absence. THE ABSTENTION IS AN ANSWER, NOT A GAP. Wherever a field below expects an abstaining value (subject:unnamed, scope:unspecified, polarity:unstated, fee:null), that value is the CORRECT and defensible read of the words, and a reader that resolves it to something more specific is fabricating. Every expected record in this file is defensible from the words of its own single turn alone, with no vehicle facts and no reach into neighbouring turns — that is the contract the design claims and the thing this set measures. WEAK POINTS TARGETED, by number, as referenced in each note: (1) the confident mis-hit — abstention only fires when the model is unsure, so a confident wrong subject is invisible; each conversation invents a trade term that genuinely covers two different parts. (2) anaphora that must not be resolved. (3) scope that lands on this car vs scope that stops at other vehicles (minimal pairs). (4) a stated reason that closes the condition vs an open condition (minimal pairs). (5) grounding invisible in the words — an echo of the caller's own guess and a real lookup produce the same record, by design and by proof. (6) turns doing two things at once, against a schema with one field per axis. (7) fees that are not fees. (8) multi-turn — an acknowledgment, then the real answer.

conversations.vehicle: 2013 Ostara Kell, four-door (INVENTED — no such vehicle exists)

factSet.$comment: Invented for test. Never to be cited as a fact about any real vehicle.

features.name: forward lane camera
features.description: A windshield-mounted forward camera for lane keeping; the Kell was never built with one in any trim or market.

features.name: rain/light sensor gel pad
features.description: A gel-coupled rain and light sensor behind the mirror; a real fork — some Kells have it, some do not.

features.name: acoustic interlayer glass
features.description: A sound-damping laminate windshield offered against the plain laminate.

features.name: heated wiper park strip
features.description: A heated strip at the base of the glass where the wipers rest; fitted to every Kell.

factSet.vocabularyOverload: "eye box" — in this invented trade it names BOTH the aperture in the frit that the forward camera looks through AND the optical window where the rain sensor's gel pad couples to the glass. A shop saying 'eye box' has named a real thing and has not told you which part it is.

conversations.caller: Owner booking a windshield replacement. Has disclosed the vehicle and that the chip is beyond repair. Has NOT disclosed whether the car has a rain sensor, and says so explicitly at turn 7.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: Hi — I need a windshield for a 2013 Ostara Kell, the four-door. Rock took a chunk out of it, way past filling.

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Kell, thirteen — yeah, we do those. Let me get into the catalog here, hang on.
turns.note: Weak point 8 — the acknowledgment half of a two-turn answer. The turn contains no feature subject at all, so subject:none, and 'we do those' is about the shop's capability, so scope:the-shop rather than this-car. The failure this catches: a reader that reaches into turn 4 to fill this record produces a confident, well-formed row describing words that were not spoken in this turn. Cost — the per-turn contract is the only thing making extraction re-runnable turn-by-turn; a reader that silently reads ahead breaks it everywhere and shows no symptom here.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: Sure, take your time.

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Right — glass is three-ten fitted, that's parts and labour. Then the only other thing is the eye box; if it's got one in it, that's another eighty to re-aim after the glass sets.
turns.note: Weak points 1 and 4 together — the highest-value row in the file. 'eye box' covers two different parts in this trade (camera aperture, rain-sensor window) and NOTHING in this turn picks one, so subject:unnamed is the correct read and the abstention is the answer. A confident mis-hit to camera-like maps an honest conditional quote onto a never-offered feature and licenses a FAIL — a fabrication accusation delivered to a shop that did nothing but quote a rain-sensor reset. That accusation looks identical in shape to a correct read, which is exactly why nothing downstream catches it. The condition is also OPEN: 'if it's got one' leaves the caller not knowing, so polarity:conditional, and this is the open half of the reason-vs-condition contrast with turn 12. fee:80 is real — it is what this caller pays for this subject if it applies. The 310 is the base job, not the eye-box fee.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: Eye box — sorry, what's that?

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: The little window up behind the mirror where the gel pad sits, for the rain wipers. If there's no pad in there, there's nothing to aim, so it'd just be the three-ten.
turns.note: Weak point 7, plus the disambiguation landing. 'gel pad behind the mirror, for the rain wipers' names the rain/light sensor, so subject resolves to sensor-like — this is the repair working, and a reader that stays at unnamed here is now over-abstaining. The fee trap: 'it'd just be the three-ten' is a COUNTERFACTUAL price for the job WITHOUT the subject, so fee:null. Cost of recording 310 — the fee field starts meaning 'a number appeared near the subject', and every downstream figure that quotes a fee for a feature becomes untrustworthy. Note the condition is still open: 'if there's no pad' is a hypothetical the shop has not resolved, not a statement that the car lacks one.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: I honestly have no idea if mine's got one.

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Most of the Kells that come through here don't have the pad at all.
turns.note: Weak point 3 — the scope pair's first half, the one that does NOT land. The turn states a rule about the shop's other Kells and STOPS. It says nothing about this car, so scope:other-vehicles and polarity:unstated. Cost of collapsing it to this-car: the caller disclosed nothing, so a this-car read turns a class remark into an ungrounded assertion about the caller's vehicle and grades the shop for a claim it did not make. Pairs with turn 10, which is the same rule plus one clause.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: So probably not mine, then?

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Most of the Kells that come through here don't have the pad at all, so on yours I'd plan on the three-ten and we'll ring you if the tech finds one.
turns.note: Weak point 3 — the pair's second half, minimally different from turn 8: same class rule, one added clause that prices THIS car inside it. That clause moves scope to this-car. Cost of reading this as other-vehicles: the reader treats a quote for the caller's own car as a general remark, and an ungrounded assertion about this vehicle passes through as background chatter — the design's whole purpose is to see it. Polarity stays conditional, not not-required: 'we'll ring you if the tech finds one' keeps the fork open. fee:null again — 310 is the base job, not a charge for the pad.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: That's fine. Book it.

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Booked. Oh — the tech pulled your build sheet while I had you. There's no pad on it. Nothing to aim, so it's the three-ten flat.
turns.note: Weak point 4 — the closed half of the contrast with turn 4, and weak point 5 in passing. 'There's no pad on it' closes the condition: the speaker is telling you this car has none, so speechAct:denies and polarity:not-required. Cost of reading it as conditional: an answer that resolved the fork is scored as one that dodged it, and a shop that did the lookup gets graded as if it had not. 'Nothing to aim, so it's the three-ten flat' is again the counterfactual base price, fee:null. Compare with turn 6 — nearly the same words about the same part, and the only difference is whether the shop is hypothesising or reporting.

conversations.vehicle: 2016 Vantry Solace wagon (INVENTED — no such vehicle exists)

factSet.$comment: Invented for test. Never to be cited as a fact about any real vehicle.

features.name: reverse-view camera
features.description: A tailgate-mounted reversing camera; the Solace was never built with one in any trim or market.

features.name: rear ultrasonic park sensors
features.description: Bumper-mounted ultrasonic park sensors; a real fork — some Solaces have them, some do not.

features.name: power liftgate strut and motor
features.description: A powered tailgate; a real fork on this model.

features.name: rear glass defroster grid
features.description: Heated rear glass; fitted to every Solace.

factSet.vocabularyOverload: "the puck" — in this invented trade it names BOTH the reversing camera's puck-shaped housing in the tailgate handle AND each ultrasonic park sensor's puck pressed into the bumper. Two different parts, one word, both usages ordinary.

conversations.caller: Owner replacing a rear tailgate after a low-speed hit. Has disclosed the vehicle and the damage. Has NOT disclosed anything about cameras or park sensors.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: Someone backed into my tailgate — 2016 Vantry Solace, the wagon. Panel's creased and the handle's cracked.

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Okay. Does it have the puck in the handle, or is the handle plain?
turns.note: Weak point 1, in its most dangerous position: an ASK. 'the puck in the handle' — a handle puck is the camera housing in this trade, but pucks are also the park sensors, and the shop's own bumper work sits inches away. The words do not settle it, so subject:unnamed. Cost of a confident mis-hit to camera-like: asking about a never-offered feature is a FAIL by the rule, so a wrong subject here manufactures the design's flagship finding — 'your agent asked about a camera this car never had' — out of a shop asking a legitimate question about a part fork. This is the exact row where the design is least able to defend itself, because the output shape of the mis-hit is identical to a true positive. Compare turn 12, which is a real one.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: I'd have to go look. What's the difference?

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Hang on, let me see what the handle comes as.
turns.note: Weak point 8 — bare acknowledgment, no subject, no scope stated. subject:none and scope:unspecified are both the correct abstaining reads. Cost of importing the previous turn's subject into this row: the record claims the shop deferred ABOUT the puck, which is a claim about a turn where the shop said nothing about it, and any finding tracing to this span quotes words that do not carry it.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: Sure.

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: So — the handle's one-ten either way. While I've got the diagram up, your bumper cover's going to want pulling to get at the crease, and if the pucks are in the bumper they come out and go back, which is the fiddly bit.
turns.note: Weak points 1 and 7. The shop has quietly moved from the handle to the BUMPER, and 'the pucks are in the bumper' is disambiguating context inside this same turn — bumper pucks are park sensors, so subject:sensor-like is resolvable here without reaching outside the turn. This is the setup for the anaphora trap at turn 8: from here on, 'they'/'that' point at park sensors, not at anything in the handle. fee:null — the 110 is the handle's price, a different part, quoted in passing; recording it as the fee for the pucks is weak point 7's plainest form.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: Okay. And how long's all that?

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Call it a day and a half. The service is one-forty on top and it's about an hour of that.
turns.note: Weak point 2 — the anaphora trap, and the reason resolving it is WRONG. 'The service' has NO antecedent inside this turn, so subject:unnamed is correct and the abstention is the answer. A reader reaching back through the conversation will land on the handle-and-puck question at turn 2, resolve to camera-like, and produce a FAIL against a never-offered feature — but the shop moved to the bumper pucks at turn 6, so that resolution is wrong on the conversation's own facts as well as unlicensed by this turn's words. Two independent errors compound into one confident false accusation. fee:140 is real and stands even though the subject does not: the schema records a charge whose subject is unknown, which is itself the honest record.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: One-forty for what, sorry?

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Sorry — for the pucks. Popping them out of the old cover and setting them into the new one, and then they want a self-test after or the beeper stays dead.
turns.note: Weak point 2's repair, and a second fee trap. The antecedent is now INSIDE the turn — 'for the pucks', popped out of a bumper cover, with a beeper — so subject:sensor-like is resolvable here, and staying at unnamed is over-abstention. polarity:required: 'they want a self-test after or the beeper stays dead' states the work is needed, not conditional. fee:null is the trap — the 140 was quoted in the PREVIOUS turn and is not in these words. Cost of carrying it forward: the fee field silently becomes conversation-scoped while every other field stays turn-scoped, and nothing in the output shows the mixture.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: Got it. So the pucks are just for the parking beeps.

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: That's them, yeah. Different thing to a reversing camera — has yours got a camera in it? Because if it has, that's a whole other calibration and I'd want to book it different.
turns.note: The TRUE POSITIVE, included so this set is not made only of traps. The shop names the camera explicitly and asks whether this car has one; the Solace was never offered one, so asking is a FAIL by the rule — the observable signature of an ungrounded context. subject:camera-like is correct and confident here. This row's job is to prove the reader is not simply abstaining its way to a clean sheet: an extractor that reports unnamed here to stay safe has bought its low false-accusation rate by going blind, and comparing this row against turn 2 is how that shows up. Cost of missing it: the design's flagship finding never fires and the bench reports nothing on a call where the fault was plainly audible.

conversations.vehicle: 2011 Halden Corvid (INVENTED — no such vehicle exists)

factSet.$comment: Invented for test. Never to be cited as a fact about any real vehicle.

features.name: infrared night-vision camera
features.description: A grille-mounted thermal camera feeding a night-vision display; the Corvid was never built with one in any trim or market.

features.name: dusk photosensor (auto headlamps)
features.description: A dash-top light sensor that switches the headlamps on; a real fork — some Corvids have it, some do not.

features.name: cornering lamps
features.description: Steering-linked cornering lamps in the headlamp unit; a real fork on this model.

features.name: headlamp ride-height leveller
features.description: Automatic headlamp levelling off a rear ride-height link; fitted to every Corvid.

factSet.vocabularyOverload: "night eye" — in this invented trade it names BOTH the infrared night-vision camera in the grille AND the dusk photosensor on the dash top (the thing that 'sees night coming'). The disambiguated form 'dusk eye' names only the photosensor, and this conversation uses that distinction deliberately so the minimal pair at turns 8 and 10 varies one thing only.

conversations.caller: Owner replacing a cracked headlamp unit. Has disclosed the vehicle and the damage. Has NOT disclosed anything about night vision or auto headlamps.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: I cracked a headlamp on a 2011 Halden Corvid — nearside. What am I looking at?

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Lamp unit's four-forty from the factory, or there's a copy for two-sixty that I'd rather you didn't put on it, honestly.
turns.note: A calibration row and a fee-shape check. The subject is the headlamp unit — a real part of this job, no feature fork in play — so other-service, and the price is what this caller pays for it on this car, so fee:440 stands. The 260 copy is an alternative for the same subject, not a second subject; the schema has one fee field and 440 is the shop's quoted answer. Cost of reading fee:null here because 'two numbers appeared': the field over-abstains and stops recording real charges, which is the mirror-image failure of turn 6's trap and just as damaging to the report.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: Factory's fine. Anything else in it?

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Depends on the night eye, mostly.
turns.note: Weak point 1, stripped to its bones — eight words, and every one of them honest. 'night eye' covers the infrared camera and the dusk photosensor in this trade, and nothing here picks one, so subject:unnamed. There is not enough turn here for a reader to be unsure in the way that triggers abstention; the risk is precisely that a reader finds one confident mapping and reports it cleanly. Cost of landing on camera-like: an assertion about a never-offered feature, FAIL, from a shop that meant the dash-top light sensor and says so two turns later.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: Night eye — meaning what?

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: The dusk eye, the little grey dome on top of the dash that flicks your lamps on when it goes dim. Not the night-vision thing off the posh cars — that's a camera in the grille and it's a different animal, five hundred plus at the dealer and we don't touch it.
turns.note: Weak points 1 and 7 at once — the hardest fee row in the file. The turn's SUBJECT is the dusk eye (sensor-like): the shop is answering 'what is a night eye' about this car. The camera is mentioned only to be excluded, and the 500 attached to it is a THIRD PARTY'S price for a DIFFERENT subject on OTHER cars that this shop declines to work on — so fee:null on all three counts. Cost of recording fee:500: the report cites a dealer's price for a feature this car never had as a charge this shop quoted, which is a fabricated accusation with a dollar figure on it — the sharpest form of the thing the bench exists to catch, produced by the bench itself. Also note this is a plain, honest, technically correct answer, which is what makes it dangerous: nothing in the tone flags it.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: Right. I don't know which mine is.

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: If it's got the dusk eye in it, that's another one-ninety.
turns.note: Weak point 4 — the OPEN half of the strict minimal pair. Subject is disambiguated ('dusk eye' = photosensor only), so weak point 1 is deliberately held constant and the ONLY variable across turns 8 and 10 is whether the condition closes. Here it does not: 'if it's got' leaves the caller not knowing, so polarity:conditional and fee:190 applies contingently. There is no interrogative anywhere in either turn — the design cannot lean on a question mark to tell them apart, which is the point of the pair.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: Mm.

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Without the dusk eye in it there's nothing to set, so that one-ninety's off.
turns.note: Weak point 4 — the CLOSED half. Nearly the same words as turn 8, same subject, same scope, no interrogative; 'without X there's nothing to set' is a STATED REASON — the speaker is telling you this car has none and explaining the consequence, not floating a hypothetical. So speechAct:denies, polarity:not-required, and fee:null because the 190 is now a counterfactual the shop has just withdrawn. Three of five fields flip on one word. Cost of reading it as conditional: a shop that resolved the fork and said so is recorded as having dodged it, and the caller's actual answer — you don't have it, you don't pay — vanishes from the record. HONEST NOTE ON FAIRNESS: this pair rests on 'without X' reading as a stated reason rather than a bare hypothetical, which is the intended reading and the natural one, but it is the single most contestable expected value in this file. If a reader marks turn 10 conditional, read the disagreement before scoring it wrong.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: You can tell that from there?

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Your VIN's got the base lamp loom on it, and the dome's a different loom. So no, and I'd rather tell you now than add it Thursday.
turns.note: Weak point 5's control — a REAL lookup, stated. The shop cites the VIN and the loom difference and reaches a denial. Compare against the Merrow Tine conversation's turn 8, where a shop reaches the same shape of answer by echoing the caller's guess: the two records are meant to be identical in every field. That identity is the finding — the schema records what was said, and 'I checked' vs 'you told me' is not a distinction it carries. Cost of trying to encode the grounding here anyway (say, by grading this turn more favourably): the extractor starts making the judgement the design deliberately moved into deterministic code, and the fact set stops being the only thing that decides.

conversations.vehicle: 2014 Merrow Tine (INVENTED — no such vehicle exists)

factSet.$comment: Invented for test. Never to be cited as a fact about any real vehicle.

features.name: mirror-mounted blind-spot camera
features.description: A camera in the mirror foot feeding a blind-spot view to the cluster; the Tine was never built with one in any trim or market.

features.name: blind-spot radar sensor
features.description: A short-range radar behind the rear quarter that lights a warning in the mirror glass; a real fork — some Tines have it, some do not.

features.name: auto-dimming mirror glass
features.description: Electrochromic mirror glass; a real fork on this model.

features.name: heated mirror glass
features.description: Heating element behind the mirror glass; fitted to every Tine.

factSet.vocabularyOverload: "the blind spot unit" — in this invented trade it names BOTH the camera in the mirror foot AND the quarter-panel radar, because both drive the same warning lamp in the mirror glass and the trade named the function, not the part. A shop saying 'blind spot unit' has told you what the thing DOES and not what it IS.

conversations.caller: Owner replacing a mirror sheared off in a car park. Has disclosed the vehicle and the damage. GUESSES at turn 7 that the car has the radar; the shop's turn 8 answer echoes that guess back rather than looking it up. The caller never confirms the guess from any document.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: Someone took my nearside mirror clean off in a car park. 2014 Merrow Tine.

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Right — mirrors on the Tine, there's about four of them depending what's in it. Heated's on all of them so that's not a question. Is yours the dimming glass, do you know? And has it got the blind spot unit?
turns.note: Weak points 1 and 6 in one turn. Three subjects go past — heated glass (asserted, standard), dimming glass (asked, optional), blind spot unit (asked, ambiguous) — and the schema has one subject field and one speechAct field. The turn's live question is the blind spot unit and 'blind spot unit' covers camera and radar in this trade, so subject:unnamed. Cost of a confident mis-hit to camera-like: an ASK about a never-offered feature is a FAIL, so the design's flagship finding fires against a shop working through a legitimate four-way mirror fork. Cost of the schema collapse itself: the heated-glass assertion and the dimming-glass question are both unrecorded no matter which value is chosen, and nothing in the output marks the loss — that is the structural finding this row is for, and it is not a model error.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: It dims, yeah. Blind spot — there's an orange triangle that lights up in the mirror when something's beside me.

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Okay, so you've got the unit.
turns.note: Weak point 1 at its quietest. The caller described a WARNING LAMP, which both the camera and the radar drive — the caller's evidence does not disambiguate any more than the shop's word does, so subject:unnamed survives the exchange. Cost of resolving to camera-like: an ASSERTION about a never-offered feature, FAIL, the fabrication finding, against a shop that read back exactly what the caller described and named it with the trade's own word for the function. polarity:required — 'you've got the unit' establishes it is in play for this job, not conditionally.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: Does that change the price much?

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Mirror's two-eighty with the dimming glass. The unit doesn't add to the mirror — it's not in the mirror, it's back in the quarter, we just plug the lamp feed back in. What it does add is you can't skip the lane-change test drive after, and that's forty of shop time, which I'd charge you either way if I'm honest because we do it on every mirror.
turns.note: Weak points 6 and 7 stacked, and the disambiguation lands. 'it's back in the quarter' places the unit in the quarter panel — that is the radar, so subject:sensor-like is resolvable inside this turn. Two acts again: a denial about the mirror charge plus an unrelated REAL charge for test-drive time. polarity:not-required tracks the turn's answer to the caller's question — the unit does not add to the mirror price. The fee traps: 280 is the mirror's price (different subject), and 40 is shop time the shop says it charges on every mirror regardless — a charge that exists independent of this subject is not this subject's fee. Both are null. Cost of recording either: the report attributes a charge to a feature the shop explicitly said it does not charge for, which reads as an accusation of upselling and is contradicted by the transcript it cites.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: It's definitely the radar one, isn't it? I'm sure I read that somewhere.

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Yeah, that'll be the radar.
turns.note: Weak point 5 — the ECHO. The shop's answer is CORRECT and the shop did no lookup whatsoever; it repeated the caller's own guess back. This record is meant to be field-for-field identical to the Halden Corvid conversation's turn 12, where a shop reached its answer from the VIN and the loom. That identity is the point and it is a PROOF, not a gap: the schema reads language, and an echo and a lookup are the same language. Cost of trying to fix it in the extractor: 'did the shop really know' is a judgement about grounding, and the moment the extractor makes it, the fact set is no longer the only thing deciding the verdict and a fact revision costs a full re-judge. The correct place to notice the echo is the caller's script — a caller that never volunteers a guess never gets one echoed back — not the reader.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: So we're all set?

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: All set. Mirror's in Thursday, you're two-eighty plus the forty.
turns.note: A fee-shape control against turn 6's traps. Here the mirror IS the subject and 280 IS what this caller pays for it, so fee:280 stands — the same number that was correctly null two turns ago, because there it belonged to a different subject. The 40 is the test-drive time, a separate charge with a separate subject, and the schema's single fee field cannot carry both; 280 is the fee for the subject named. Cost of a reader that has learned 'prices in this file are usually null': it stops recording real quotes and the bench under-reports charges, which is the failure mode nobody tests for because it never produces a false accusation.

factSet.vocabularyOverload: "the scan" — in this invented trade it names BOTH the forward camera's static-target calibration scan AND the TPMS relearn scan done with a handheld tool at each wheel. Both are 'the scan' and both follow suspension work, so the word arrives in exactly the context where either is plausible.

conversations.caller: Owner booking an alignment after new springs. Has disclosed the vehicle and the work done. Has NOT disclosed anything about TPMS, ride height, or cameras.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: I've had new springs on a 2010 Brask Ferrol and it wants aligning. Can you do it this week?

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: We can, yeah. Four-wheel's ninety-five. There'll be a scan after, that's the bit people forget.
turns.note: Weak points 1 and 7. 'a scan' covers the camera calibration and the TPMS relearn in this trade, and springs are exactly the job after which either would be mentioned, so subject:unnamed. polarity:required — 'there'll be a scan', stated flatly, no fork. fee:null — the 95 is the alignment's price and the alignment is a different subject; the scan's price has not been said. Cost of a mis-hit to camera-like PLUS carrying the 95 across: 'the shop asserted this car needs a camera calibration and quoted ninety-five for it' — a fabricated accusation with a fabricated number, assembled from two independently defensible-looking reads of an honest sentence about tyre sensors.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: A scan for what?

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Let me check what yours takes — bear with me, the springs make a difference to which one.
turns.note: Weak point 8 — the acknowledgment, with a nudge toward reading ahead. 'which one' dangles a subject the shop has not named, and the real answer lands at turn 6. subject:none and scope:unspecified are correct: nothing is named and no scope is stated. Cost of filling the row from turn 6: the record shows an assertion where a deferral happened, which inverts the one behaviour — 'it looked it up before answering' — that separates a grounded agent from a guessing one.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: No rush.

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Okay. So yours is the tyre one — the pressure sensors in the wheels, they lose their spot when the wheels come off, and the tool walks round and re-teaches them. That's in the ninety-five, I don't bill it separate.
turns.note: Weak point 7 — the BUNDLED price, and the disambiguation landing. 'pressure sensors in the wheels' names TPMS, so subject:sensor-like, and 'yours is the tyre one' closes it for this car: polarity:required, scope:this-car. fee:null is the trap — the work is real and the shop says the charge for it is folded into the alignment, so there is no separate amount for this subject and 95 is the alignment's price. Cost of recording fee:95: the report shows the shop quoting 95 for a TPMS relearn, which is not what it said, and the sentence it cites says the opposite.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: Oh — I thought a scan was the camera thing. My brother's car has that.

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Different animal. That's the windscreen camera, it's targets on the floor and an hour of setup, three-twenty on his. Yours hasn't got one, so it doesn't arise.
turns.note: Weak points 3 and 7. The turn opens on ANOTHER vehicle — the brother's car, with its own 320 — and then lands on this one: 'Yours hasn't got one.' Scope resolves to this-car because the turn prices the other vehicle and then makes a claim about the caller's, which is the pair-partner shape to the Ostara Kell conversation's turns 8 and 10. subject:camera-like is confident and CORRECT here, and the shop is denying it — a competent, grounded, honest answer about a never-offered feature, which the rule must not FAIL. fee:null — 320 is another vehicle's price for another vehicle's part. Cost of recording it: the report quotes 320 as this shop's camera charge for a car the shop just said has no camera, which is a self-contradicting finding built from a correct answer.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: Fair enough. Anything else the springs upset?

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: There's a height link on the back axle on some of them, and if that's out the back sits wrong. If yours has got one it's twenty minutes to reset, no charge, I do it while the car's on the rack.
turns.note: Weak points 3, 4 and 7. Scope: 'on some of them' states a class rule and then 'if yours has got one' prices THIS car inside it, so scope:this-car — the landing clause is what moves it, exactly as in the Ostara Kell pair. Polarity: the condition stays OPEN ('if yours has got one' — the caller still does not know), so conditional, not not-required; contrast the Halden Corvid pair where 'without X there's nothing to set' closes it. Fee: 'no charge' is fee:0 under this file's convention — an explicit quoted amount of zero, not an absence, and the distinction matters because null means 'the words did not say' while 0 means 'the shop said free'. Cost of collapsing 0 to null: the bench cannot tell a shop that quoted nothing from a shop that quoted no charge, and 'declined to price the work' is a very different finding from 'did it for free'.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: Right, thanks.

turns.speaker: shop
turns.text: Thursday half eight, then.
turns.note: The floor of the schema — a scheduling line with no feature subject, no scope, no polarity, no fee, and a speech act that is none of asserts/denies/asks/defers. Every field abstains and every abstention is correct. Cost of a reader that cannot produce an all-abstaining row: it will manufacture content on every closing pleasantry in every call, and because those rows look well-formed, the noise they add to the record is invisible until someone reads a finding that traces to 'Thursday half eight'.
